content: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease that causes systemic inflammation. It is estimated to affect 0.5% to 1.0% of the population in Western countries. The disease typically manifests with joint pain, swelling, tenderness, stiffness, and deformities, which result from inflammation of the synovial lining in joints, tendons, and surrounding structures. Beyond joint involvement, RA can lead to systemic complications, including premature atherosclerosis, interstitial lung disease, pneumonitis, mononeuritis multiplex, subcutaneous nodules, and vasculitis. These systemic effects contribute to significant morbidity and a reduction in health-related quality of life (HRQoL). RA can also cause severe functional limitations, shortand long-term disability, and loss of productivity, both in the workplace and at home, leading to substantial societal costs. The treatment of RA involves a range of pharmacological options. These include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), glucocorticoids, traditional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) such as methotrexate (MTX), sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide, cyclosporine, and gold compounds, as well as biologic DMARDs like etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab, abatacept, anakinra, rituximab, certolizumab pegol, golimumab, and tocilizumab. Additionally, newer oral small-molecule drugs, such as tofacitinib, are available. DMARDs are central to RA management, as they improve pain, function, and HRQoL, reduce disability, and slow radiographic progression of joint damage. Guidelines for RA treatment, such as those from the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) and the American College of Rheumatology (ACR), recommend treatment algorithms based on disease activity and prognostic factors. These guidelines emphasize the use of traditional and biologic DMARDs, often supplemented by NSAIDs, glucocorticoids, and non-pharmacological interventions like physical and occupational therapy. Methotrexate (MTX) is the most commonly used traditional DMARD for RA and is highly effective in controlling the disease's signs and symptoms. It is typically the first-line therapy for RA and can be used alone or in combination with other DMARDs or biologic agents to enhance treatment efficacy. MTX can be administered orally or parenterally (via subcutaneous or intramuscular injection). Oral MTX is more commonly prescribed due to its convenience, but subcutaneous MTX offers advantages such as increased bioavailability and reduced gastrointestinal side effects, particularly at higher doses (e.g., 25 mg). Subcutaneous MTX is also easier to administer and less painful than intramuscular injections. Some patients who do not respond adequately to oral MTX may benefit from switching to subcutaneous administration, although the clinical significance of this remains uncertain. RA is driven by the activation and interaction of various immune cells, including T cells, B cells, and mononuclear cells, as well as other joint-resident cells like fibroblasts, osteoclasts, and chondrocytes. This immune activation leads to the overproduction of chemokines, metalloproteinases, and pro-inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) and interleukins (IL-1, IL-6). These mediators contribute to the destruction of bone and cartilage, which is a hallmark of RA. MTX exerts its anti-inflammatory effects by targeting this inflammatory cascade. Although the exact mechanism of action is not fully understood, several pathways have been proposed. These include the inhibition of T-cell proliferation through effects on purine and pyrimidine metabolism, interference with glutathione metabolism to reduce inflammatory cell recruitment, inhibition of transmethylation reactions to prevent T-cell cytotoxicity, and increased release of adenosine, an endogenous anti-inflammatory molecule. MTX undergoes intracellular polyglutamation, which inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and other folate-dependent enzymes, leading to the accumulation of AICAR (5-aminoimidazole-4-carboxamide ribonucleotide). AICAR promotes the release of adenosine, which interacts with receptors on neutrophils and mononuclear cells, contributing to MTX's anti-inflammatory effects. MTX remains the cornerstone of RA management due to its favorable balance of efficacy and safety. It is considered the gold standard for RA treatment and is often the first medication prescribed. When patients do not achieve an adequate response to MTX monotherapy, it is commonly combined with other DMARDs or biologic agents. MTX is typically initiated at a low dose and titrated to a target weekly dose of 25 mg or higher. For patients who do not respond to oral MTX, subcutaneous administration may be considered, as it offers more predictable pharmacokinetics and higher bioavailability at higher doses. Despite the widespread use of MTX, there is a need for further research to clarify the role of subcutaneous MTX in RA management, particularly given the significantly higher costs associated with biologic therapies. This systematic review aims to address this gap in knowledge and provide insights into the use of subcutaneous MTX for RA.
